claim: Vibrio cholerae causes an estimated 3 million infections and 120,000 deaths each year.
source: Vibrio cholerae (Vc) causes an estimated 3 million infections and 120,000 deaths each year, and larger and more deadly outbreaks have increased during the last decade (Camacho et al., 2018; Luquero et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Camacho et al., 2018; Luquero et al., 2016).

claim: Larger and more deadly cholera outbreaks have increased during the last decade.
source: Vibrio cholerae (Vc) causes an estimated 3 million infections and 120,000 deaths each year, and larger and more deadly outbreaks have increased during the last decade (Camacho et al., 2018; Luquero et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Camacho et al., 2018; Luquero et al., 2016).

claim: Many behaviors of V. cholerae in the aquatic environment and inside the host are significantly affected by the presence of other microbes.
source: It is nearly certain that many behaviors of Vc in the aquatic environment and inside the host are significantly affected by the presence of other microbes (Weil and Ryan, 2018), and recent studies provide evidence that the gut microbiota may impact the severity of cholera (Alavi et al., 2020; Hsiao et al., 2014; Levade et al., 2020; Midani et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Weil and Ryan, 2018).

claim: The gut microbiota may impact the severity of cholera.
source: It is nearly certain that many behaviors of Vc in the aquatic environment and inside the host are significantly affected by the presence of other microbes (Weil and Ryan, 2018), and recent studies provide evidence that the gut microbiota may impact the severity of cholera (Alavi et al., 2020; Hsiao et al., 2014; Levade et al., 2020; Midani et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Alavi et al., 2020; Hsiao et al., 2014; Levade et al., 2020; Midani et al., 2018).

claim: Disruption of the commensal microbiota with antibiotics is required to allow successful V. cholerae colonization in adult rodent models.
source: For instance, disruption of the commensal microbiota with antibiotics is required to allow successful Vc colonization in adult rodent models.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about animal models of V. cholerae infection.

claim: Starvation and streptomycin treatment are needed to reduce the intestinal normal flora to allow V. cholerae infection to occur in the cecum and the entire bowel in guinea pigs.
source: Starvation and streptomycin treatment are needed to reduce the intestinal normal flora to allow Vc infection to occur in the cecum and the entire bowel in guinea pigs (Freter, 1955).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Freter, 1955).

claim: Streptomycin treatment is needed to allow V. cholerae colonization, mainly in the cecum and large intestine, of adult mice.
source: In another case, streptomycin treatment is needed to allow Vc colonization, mainly in the cecum and large intestine, of adult mice (Nygren et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Nygren et al., 2009).

claim: V. cholerae actively employs a type VI secretion system to attack host commensal microbiota to enhance colonization of the gut in infant mice.
source: Conversely, Vc actively employs a type VI secretion system to attack host commensal microbiota to enhance colonization of the gut in infant mice (Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Zhao et al., 2018).

claim: Pre-colonization with Blautia obeum in adult gnotobiotic mice decreases the V. cholerae counts in the feces after infection.
source: Pre-colonization with Blautia obeum, an anaerobic Gram-positive bacterium, in adult gnotobiotic mice decreases the Vc counts in the feces after infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Hsiao et al., 2014) mentioned in the same paragraph.

claim: B. obeum is thought to produce a signaling molecule that induces V. cholerae into a high cell-density quorum sensing state.
source: B. obeum is thought to produce a signaling molecule that induces Vc into a high cell-density quorum sensing state (Hsiao et al., 2014) in which virulence gene expression is repressed (Jung et al., 2015; Watve et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Hsiao et al., 2014).

claim: Virulence gene expression is repressed in V. cholerae in a high cell-density quorum sensing state.
source: B. obeum is thought to produce a signaling molecule that induces Vc into a high cell-density quorum sensing state (Hsiao et al., 2014) in which virulence gene expression is repressed (Jung et al., 2015; Watve et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Jung et al., 2015; Watve et al., 2020).

claim: Certain microbiota species reduce V. cholerae colonization in germfree adult and suckling mice by producing the enzyme bile salt hydrolase that degrades the host-produced virulence-activating compound taurocholate.
source: Certain microbiota species reduce Vc colonization in germfree adult and suckling mice by producing the enzyme bile salt hydrolase that degrades the host-produced virulence-activating compound taurocholate (Alavi et al., 2020; Hsiao et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Alavi et al., 2020; Hsiao et al., 2014).

claim: Bacteroides vulgatus reduces V. cholerae proliferation within the intestine of germfree adult mice and typical laboratory infant mice through metabolizing host glycans into short-chain fatty acids that suppress V. cholerae growth.
source: Through metabolizing host glycans into short-chain fatty acids that suppress Vc growth, a prominent commensal species, Bacteroides vulgatus, reduces Vc proliferation within the intestine of germfree adult mice and typical laboratory infant mice (You et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (You et al., 2019).

claim: Paracoccus aminovorans was more abundant in the gut microbiota during V. cholerae infection.
source: We also observed that the gut microbial species Paracoccus aminovorans (Pa) was more abundant in the gut microbiota during Vc infection (Midani et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Midani et al., 2018).

claim: Most of the native gut microbiota is typically displaced by secretory diarrhea during cholera.
source: This association between Pa and Vc is unusual because most of the native gut microbiota is typically displaced by secretory diarrhea during cholera (Hsiao et al., 2014; David et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Hsiao et al., 2014; David et al., 2015).

claim: Pa interacts directly with V. cholerae to form dual-species biofilm structures with previously uncharacterized features.
source: Here, we show that Pa interacts directly with Vc to form dual-species biofilm structures with previously uncharacterized features.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including microscopy images and biofilm assays.

claim: V. cholerae colonization inside the animal host is enhanced by the presence of Pa in the small intestine.
source: Moreover, Vc colonization inside the animal host is enhanced by the presence of Pa in the small intestine, and this effect is dependent upon Vc biofilm production.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from animal studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: The enhancement of V. cholerae colonization by Pa is dependent upon V. cholerae biofilm production.
source: Moreover, Vc colonization inside the animal host is enhanced by the presence of Pa in the small intestine, and this effect is dependent upon Vc biofilm production.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from animal studies with biofilm mutants presented in the manuscript.

claim: Paracoccus is a genus of soil microbes found in low abundance in the gut microbiome of humans.
source: Paracoccus is a genus of soil microbes found in low abundance in the gut microbiome of humans (Yatsunenko et al., 2012; Urakami et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Yatsunenko et al., 2012; Urakami et al., 1990).

claim: Pa was identified as an unexpectedly abundant gut microbe during active V. cholerae infection.
source: Our previously published analysis of stool gut microbes from household contacts of cholera patients identified Pa as an unexpectedly abundant gut microbe during active Vc infection, and this organism was rarely found in uninfected participants (Midani et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Midani et al., 2018).

claim: Pa was rarely found in uninfected participants.
source: Our previously published analysis of stool gut microbes from household contacts of cholera patients identified Pa as an unexpectedly abundant gut microbe during active Vc infection, and this organism was rarely found in uninfected participants (Midani et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Midani et al., 2018).

claim: Pa abundance was significantly higher as a proportion of the total sequencing reads in the stool of infected household contacts (6/22, 27%) compared to only 5.6% (2/36) of uninfected individuals (p=0.009).
source: Pa abundance was significantly higher as a proportion of the total sequencing reads in the stool of infected household contacts (6/22, 27%) compared to only 5.6% (2/36) of uninfected individuals (Figure 1A, p=0.009 by Mann–Whitney U-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis presented in Figure 1A with statistical testing.

claim: The ratio of Pa to V. cholerae abundance present during infection was variable and averaged 1:1.
source: The ratio of Pa to Vc abundance present during infection was variable and averaged 1:1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: There is a drastic reduction of nearly all gut microbes during active V. cholerae infection due to secretory diarrhea, oral rehydration solution ingestion, and V. cholerae infection itself.
source: These findings were particularly interesting because typically there is a drastic reduction of nearly all gut microbes during active Vc infection (Hsiao et al., 2014; David et al., 2015) due to secretory diarrhea, oral rehydration solution ingestion, and Vc infection itself, and yet here Pa was found in an increased abundance in some actively infected participants.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Hsiao et al., 2014; David et al., 2015).

claim: Pa was found in an increased abundance in some actively infected participants despite the typical drastic reduction of gut microbes during active V. cholerae infection.
source: These findings were particularly interesting because typically there is a drastic reduction of nearly all gut microbes during active Vc infection (Hsiao et al., 2014; David et al., 2015) due to secretory diarrhea, oral rehydration solution ingestion, and Vc infection itself, and yet here Pa was found in an increased abundance in some actively infected participants.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the prior study (Midani et al., 2018).

claim: The V. cholerae count in Pa-colonized infected household contacts compared to non-Pa colonized household contacts was modestly higher (approximately threefold) but not statistically significant (p=0.1474).
source: The Vc count in Pa-colonized infected household contacts compared to non-Pa colonized household contacts was modestly higher (approximately threefold) in this study; however, statistically the difference was not significant (Mann–Whitney U-test, p=0.1474), which is likely due to small sample size (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Pa successfully and stably colonized the small intestines of infant mice for at least 12 hr.
source: StrepR Pa colonies (>106 CFUs/small intestine) were recovered at these two time points (Figure 2A), and no StrepR colonies were detected in the mock-treated group, indicating that Pa successfully and stably colonized the small intestines of these animals using these methods at least for 12 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Pretreatment with antibiotics was not required for Pa colonization in infant mice.
source: Unlike previous studies (Freter, 1955; Nygren et al., 2009), pretreatment with antibiotics was not required for Pa colonization (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2A and contrasts with cited previous studies.

claim: Pa colonization demonstrated no significant change in the microbial composition and diversity in the mouse small intestines.
source: Sequencing analysis of the mouse small intestines demonstrated no significant change in the microbial composition and diversity with and without Pa colonization (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: V. cholerae intestinal colonization was significantly higher (~10-fold, p≤0.0001) in mice pre-colonized with Pa compared to the control group.
source: Comparing Pa pre-colonized mice to the control group, there was a significant increase (~10-fold, p≤0.0001) of Vc colonization in the mice pre-colonized with Pa (Figure 2B) 24 hr after infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical testing presented in Figure 2B.

claim: The enhanced intestinal colonization by V. cholerae in the Pa-colonized mice was observed as early as 6 hr after infection and maintained throughout the colonization period.
source: This enhanced intestinal colonization by Vc in the Pa-colonized mice was observed as early as 6 hr after infection and maintained throughout the colonization period (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The V. cholerae:Pa ratio inside the mouse intestine at the early stage of infection (6 hr after V. cholerae infection, 18 hr after the last Pa inoculation) was variable, but was approximately 10:1.
source: Using this infection model, similar to human infection, the Vc:Pa ratio inside the mouse intestine at the early stage of infection (6 hr after Vc infection, 18 hr after the last Pa inoculation) was variable, but was approximately 10:1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: V. cholerae intestinal colonization was significantly higher when coinfected with Pa than without Pa.
source: In agreement with the results obtained with the Pa pre-colonization model, Vc intestinal colonization was significantly higher when coinfected with Pa than without Pa (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: The presence of a single gut microbiota species is sufficient to increase V. cholerae host colonization.
source: Given that Pa colonization did not overtly change the overall composition of the gut microbiota (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), collectively, our results demonstrate that the presence of a single gut microbiota species is sufficient to increase Vc host colonization.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing Pa colonization does not change gut microbiota composition but does increase V. cholerae colonization.

claim: There was a small difference (less than twofold) in growth in the planktonic phase of either V. cholerae or Pa in the co-cultures when compared to the cultures containing a single species.
source: There was a small difference (less than twofold) in growth in the planktonic phase of either Vc or Pa in the co-cultures when compared to the cultures containing a single species (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: The V. cholerae/Pa co-culture formed a pellicle that was visibly thicker and more robust than that formed by V. cholerae monoculture.
source: However, more importantly, the Vc/Pa co-culture formed a pellicle that was visibly thicker and more robust than that formed by Vc monoculture (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by visual observation and images presented in Figure 3B.

claim: The Pa monoculture did not form a visible pellicle.
source: The Pa monoculture did not form a visible pellicle.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observation.

claim: Compared to V. cholerae monoculture, the co-culture samples contained over 50-fold more V. cholerae cells while the ratio of V. cholerae to Pa approached approximately 1:1.
source: Compared to Vc monoculture, the co-culture samples contained over 50-fold more Vc cells while the ratio of Vc to Pa approached approximately 1:1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: Only a small fraction (0.01%) of V. cholerae and Pa could be washed off from the isolated pellicles.
source: Moreover, only a small fraction (0.01%) of Vc and Pa could be washed off from the isolated pellicles (Figure 3D), suggesting that these species are tightly integrated into the pellicle.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: V. cholerae and Pa are tightly integrated into the pellicle.
source: Moreover, only a small fraction (0.01%) of Vc and Pa could be washed off from the isolated pellicles (Figure 3D), suggesting that these species are tightly integrated into the pellicle.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing only a small fraction could be washed off.

claim: V. cholerae formed a more robust biofilm than Pa under pellicle-forming conditions as demonstrated by increased CV staining in wells containing V. cholerae only compared to wells containing Pa only.
source: Consistent with our pellicle compositional analysis, Vc formed a more robust biofilm than Pa under these conditions as demonstrated by increased CV staining in wells containing Vc only compared to wells containing Pa only (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: CV staining was increased in wells containing V. cholerae and live Pa compared to wells with V. cholerae only in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Importantly, CV staining was increased in wells containing Vc and live Pa compared to wells with Vc only in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: CV staining was not different in wells containing V. cholerae and heat-killed Pa compared to wells with V. cholerae only.
source: In contrast, CV staining was not different in wells containing Vc and heat-killed Pa compared to wells with Vc only (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: An increase in CV staining was observed in wells in which Pa and V. cholerae were added sequentially.
source: As in our previous results in the co-inoculation experiment, an increase in CV staining was observed in wells in which the two species were added sequentially, but not in the wells with Vc only (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Wells pre-incubated with heat-killed Pa and subsequently inoculated with V. cholerae had no increase in CV staining compared to wells inoculated with V. cholerae alone.
source: Moreover, wells pre-incubated with heat-killed Pa and subsequently inoculated with Vc had no increase in CV staining compared to wells inoculated with Vc alone (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The presence of Pa, regardless of the order of encounter, results in an enhanced biofilm formation of V. cholerae.
source: Together, our biofilm quantification data suggest that the presence of Pa, regardless of the order of encounter, results in an enhanced biofilm formation of Vc.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing enhanced biofilm formation in both co-inoculation and sequential inoculation experiments.

claim: There was no significant increase in CV staining in wells with ΔvpsL mutant and Pa co-culture when compared to wells with the ΔvpsL mutants only.
source: In contrast to our observations in culture of a vpsL+ strain, there was no significant increase in CV staining in wells with ∆vpsL mutant and Pa co-culture when compared to wells with the ∆vpsL mutants only (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: The biofilm formation defects of the V. cholerae ΔvpsL mutants and the increased biofilm formation response in the presence of Pa could be restored by the introduction of a plasmid constitutively expressing vpsL.
source: The biofilm formation defects of the Vc ∆vpsL mutants and the increased biofilm formation response in the presence of Pa could be restored by the introduction of a plasmid constitutively expressing vpsL (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The relative transcript levels of vpsL were significantly higher in the V. cholerae/Pa co-culture than that in the V. cholerae monoculture after 24–48 hr of growth.
source: Using qRT-PCR, we determined that the relative transcript levels of vpsL (the first and a representative gene in the vpsII operon in Vc) were significantly higher in the Vc/Pa co-culture than that in the Vc monoculture after 24–48 hr of growth (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: There was no significant difference in vpsL transcript levels after 72 hr of co-culture.
source: There was no significant difference in vpsL transcript levels after 72 hr of co-culture.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data.

claim: Pa induces V. cholerae biofilm gene expression when the two species are cultured together, especially at the early stage of interaction.
source: Our results suggest that Pa induces Vc biofilm gene expression when the two species are cultured together, especially at the early stage of interaction, creating the conditions for increased pellicle formation in co-cultures.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the qRT-PCR data showing increased vpsL expression in co-cultures.

claim: Healthy Pa cells and V. cholerae ΔvpsL mutant cells do not show positive VPS staining.
source: Note that for Gram-negative bacteria, including Vc and Pa, the WGA lectin molecules do not pass through the outer membrane of healthy cells. Indeed, control experiments show that healthy Pa cells and Vc ∆vpsL mutant cells do not show positive VPS staining (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by control experiments presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Extensive WGA signal is observed in V. cholerae/Pa co-culture pellicle.
source: Figure 6A shows a Vc/Pa co-culture pellicle, in which extensive WGA signal is observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: Regions with strong VPS signal are not necessarily spatially correlated with clusters of Pa cells.
source: We also noticed that regions with strong VPS signal are not necessarily spatially correlated with clusters of Pa cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy observations.

claim: In the co-cultured pellicle vspL expression is elevated in subpopulations of V. cholerae cells.
source: Figure 6C shows that in the co-cultured pellicle vspL expression is elevated in subpopulations of Vc cells in the co-culture.
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: The physical presence of Pa in the co-culture pellicle augments the production of VPS in V. cholerae cells, leading to increased V. cholerae biofilm formation.
source: Together, these results suggest that the physical presence of Pa in the co-culture pellicle augments the production of VPS in Vc cells, leading to increased Vc biofilm formation; the Pa cells, in turn, require VPS to be integrated into the 3D structure of the pellicle.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the microscopy and biofilm data.

claim: Pa cells require VPS to be integrated into the 3D structure of the pellicle.
source: Together, these results suggest that the physical presence of Pa in the co-culture pellicle augments the production of VPS in Vc cells, leading to increased Vc biofilm formation; the Pa cells, in turn, require VPS to be integrated into the 3D structure of the pellicle.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing Pa integration depends on VPS production.

claim: Biofilm-grown V. cholerae cells are more infectious in humans due to increased resistance to gastric pH and higher expression of virulence factors compared to planktonically grown cells.
source: Biofilm-grown Vc cells are known to be more infectious in humans due to increased resistance to gastric pH and higher expression of virulence factors (e.g., such as the toxin co-regulated pilus, which mediates host colonization) compared to planktonically grown cells (Tamayo et al., 2010; Gallego-Hernandez et al., 2020; Zhu and Mekalanos, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Tamayo et al., 2010; Gallego-Hernandez et al., 2020; Zhu and Mekalanos, 2003).

claim: There was a modest increase in the expression of ctxA and tcpA virulence genes in the V. cholerae/Pa co-culture compared to the V. cholerae monoculture.
source: As expected, ctxA and tcpA relative transcript levels were low in all samples; however, there was a modest increase in the expression of these two virulence genes in the Vc/Pa co-culture compared to the Vc monoculture (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ΔvpsL mutant was able to colonize the mouse small intestine as well as the WT vpsL+ strain when V. cholerae was administered to the animals alone.
source: As shown previously (Fong et al., 2010), the ∆vpsL mutant was able to colonize the mouse small intestine as well as the WT vpsL+ strain, confirming that VPS is not absolutely required for host colonization when Vc was administered to the animals alone.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to published literature (Fong et al., 2010).

claim: VPS is not absolutely required for host colonization when V. cholerae was administered to the animals alone.
source: As shown previously (Fong et al., 2010), the ∆vpsL mutant was able to colonize the mouse small intestine as well as the WT vpsL+ strain, confirming that VPS is not absolutely required for host colonization when Vc was administered to the animals alone.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to published literature (Fong et al., 2010).

claim: While Pa increased WT vpsL+ V. cholerae colonization, the ΔvpsL mutant did not exhibit the enhanced colonization phenotype in the Pa pre-colonized mice.
source: In contrast, while Pa increased WT vpsL+ Vc colonization, the ∆vpsL mutant did not exhibit the enhanced colonization phenotype in the Pa pre-colonized mice (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7A.

claim: Host colonization enhancement caused by Pa pre-colonization could be restored in the ΔvpsL mutants with a plasmid constitutively expressing vpsL, but not with the empty vector.
source: Host colonization enhancement caused by Pa pre-colonization could be restored in the ∆vpsL mutants with a plasmid constitutively expressing vpsL, but not with the empty vector (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: When V. cholerae ΔvpsL mutants were coinfected with Pa, there was no increase in host colonization.
source: Similar results were observed using the co-infection model; when Vc ∆vpsL mutants were coinfected with Pa, there was no increase in host colonization (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7B.

claim: The enhancement of V. cholerae intestinal colonization in the presence Pa is dependent on the VPS.
source: Together, we concluded that the enhancement of Vc intestinal colonization in the presence Pa is dependent on the VPS, consistent with our in vitro data.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data with ΔvpsL mutants.

claim: Cell–cell adhesion, conferred by RbmA, is more important than cell–surface adhesion conferred by RbmC/Bap1 for the enhancement of V. cholerae biofilm by Pa.
source: Specifically, we showed that cell–cell adhesion, conferred by RbmA, is more important than cell–surface adhesion conferred by RbmC/Bap1.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data with biofilm mutants.

claim: When compared to the wells containing the ΔrbmA mutant alone, the CV staining was higher in the wells with the ΔrbmA mutant co-cultured with Pa.
source: When compared to the wells containing the ∆rbmA mutant alone, the CV staining was higher in the wells with the ∆rbmA mutant co-cultured with Pa.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The increase in CV staining was not as high in the ΔrbmA mutant/Pa co-culture compared to that in WT V. cholerae/Pa co-culture.
source: However, the increase was not as high in the ∆rbmA mutant/Pa co-culture compared to that in WT Vc/Pa co-culture (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7C.

claim: The presence of Pa did not increase CV staining in the wells containing the ΔrbmC Δbap1 mutants.
source: Furthermore, the presence of Pa did not increase CV staining in the wells containing the ∆rbmC ∆bap1 mutants (Figure 7C) because the ∆rbmC ∆bap1 mutant is not able to adhere to the interface.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7C.

claim: The ΔrbmC Δbap1 mutant is not able to adhere to the interface.
source: Furthermore, the presence of Pa did not increase CV staining in the wells containing the ∆rbmC ∆bap1 mutants (Figure 7C) because the ∆rbmC ∆bap1 mutant is not able to adhere to the interface.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about the function of RbmC and Bap1.

claim: ΔrbmA mutants did not show any increase in host colonization when coinfected with Pa.
source: In agreement with our in vitro results, while host colonization was significantly higher for WT Vc coinfected with Pa than without Pa (Figure 2C), ∆rbmA mutants did not show any increase in host colonization when coinfected with Pa, and ∆rbmC ∆bap1 mutants demonstrated increased colonization with Pa but less colonization compared with WT Vc co-infection with Pa (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7B.

claim: ΔrbmC Δbap1 mutants demonstrated increased colonization with Pa but less colonization compared with WT V. cholerae co-infection with Pa.
source: In agreement with our in vitro results, while host colonization was significantly higher for WT Vc coinfected with Pa than without Pa (Figure 2C), ∆rbmA mutants did not show any increase in host colonization when coinfected with Pa, and ∆rbmC ∆bap1 mutants demonstrated increased colonization with Pa but less colonization compared with WT Vc co-infection with Pa (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7B.

claim: The ability of V. cholerae to form a structurally intact biofilm is important for the enhancement of colonization facilitated by the presence of Pa.
source: These results indicate that the ability of Vc to form a structurally intact biofilm is important for the enhancement of colonization facilitated by the presence of Pa.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data with biofilm mutants.

claim: V. cholerae is known to form a clonal community in both in vitro and in vivo biofilms and these are known to exclude other species, including even planktonic V. cholerae cells.
source: This is unexpected because Vc is known to form a clonal community in both in vitro and in vivo biofilms and these are known to exclude other species, including even planktonic Vc cells (Millet, 2014; Nadell et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Millet, 2014; Nadell et al., 2015).

claim: V. cholerae and Pa coexist stably in the pellicle structure.
source: In summary, we found that Vc and Pa coexist stably in the pellicle structure and this relationship may explain the mechanism by which Pa resists displacement in humans during active Vc infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing both species in pellicles.

claim: The coexistence of V. cholerae and Pa in pellicle structure may explain the mechanism by which Pa resists displacement in humans during active V. cholerae infection.
source: In summary, we found that Vc and Pa coexist stably in the pellicle structure and this relationship may explain the mechanism by which Pa resists displacement in humans during active Vc infection.
evidence: This claim is speculative, connecting in vitro findings to human observations.

claim: Pa cells exist mainly at the pellicle–liquid interface, with clusters of Pa cells penetrating into the interior of the pellicle.
source: (D) Cross-sectional views of the region shown in (C), at the bottom of the pellicle. Pa cells exist mainly at the pellicle–liquid interface, with clusters of Pa cells penetrating into the interior of the pellicle.
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: A gut bacterium in the genus Blautia was recently found to encode functions that confer colonization resistance (e.g., bile salt hydrolase) to V. cholerae infection.
source: For instance, a gut bacterium in the genus Blautia was recently found to encode functions that confer colonization resistance (e.g., bile salt hydrolase) to Vc infection (Alavi et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Alavi et al., 2020).

claim: A species in the genus Blautia is correlated with decreased susceptibility to V. cholerae infection.
